chi-square-setup-s1.title: Age and main news source
chi-square-setup-s1.text: A polling firm asks a random sample of 400 adults in a large city for their age group and the source they use most for news. (Invented data.)

table.caption: Observed counts: age group by main news source

chi-square-setup-s2.title: Getting to school at three high schools
chi-square-setup-s2.text: A district takes a separate random sample of students at each of its three high schools and asks how they usually get to school. (Invented data.)

table.caption: Observed counts: school by travel mode

items.q: Which test fits the firm's question of whether age group and main news source are related?

why.correct: One sample, two categorical variables: independence.
options: That compares two proportions. Here each variable has three categories.
Right: one random sample, two categorical variables recorded on each person.
That looks at one category of one variable and ignores age.
Homogeneity compares one variable across separate samples or groups. Here one sample is classified two ways.
A two-sample z test for $p_1 - p_2$
A chi-square test for independence
A one-proportion z test for the share who use TV
A chi-square test for homogeneity

why.correct: $H_0$: the variables are independent (no association) in the population; $H_a$: they are associated.
options: These are reversed. The null hypothesis is "no association".
The hypotheses are about the whole relationship, not one cell, and $H_0$ is the "no association" claim.
Right: independence hypotheses are about the relationship between the two variables in the population.
That is about one variable only. The question is whether the two variables are related.
$H_0$: there is an association; $H_a$: there is no association
$H_0$: older adults in the city prefer TV news; $H_a$: older adults in the city do not prefer TV news
$H_0$: age group and news source are not associated among the city's adults; $H_a$: they are associated
$H_0$: the proportions of adults in the three age groups are equal; $H_a$: they are not

items.q: If $H_0$ is true, what is the expected count of adults aged 55 and older whose main source is TV?

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. The expected count is what $H_0$ predicts: row total times column total over the grand total.
That splits 400 equally over the nine cells. Expected counts follow the row and column totals.
That splits the 55 and older row equally over the three sources. Under $H_0$ the row follows the overall column pattern.

items.q: Write the expression for the expected count of adults aged 18 to 34 whose main source is news websites, then give its value.

mistakes.why: That uses the social media or TV column total, 130. The news websites column total is 140.
Multiply the row and column totals, then divide by the grand total.

items.q: Which statement correctly checks the large counts condition for this chi-square test?

why.correct: Large counts for chi-square: all expected counts at least 5.
options: Comparing $n$ with 30 is a rule for means.
Right: a chi-square test needs every expected count to be at least 5.
They always add to the grand total, so this checks nothing.
The condition is about expected counts, and the chi-square threshold is 5.
The sample of 400 is at least 30
The smallest expected count is 39, so every expected count is at least 5
The expected counts add up to 400, the sample size
The smallest observed count is 18, so the observed counts are at least 10

items.q: Which test fits the district's question of whether the travel mode distributions differ among the schools?

why.correct: Several samples or groups, one categorical variable: homogeneity.
options: Right: three separate random samples, one categorical variable compared across them.
Independence uses one sample classified by two variables. Here the district chose how many students to sample at each school.
Separate tests for one category at a time would not compare the whole distributions at once.
That compares two schools on one category. There are three schools and three categories.
A chi-square test for homogeneity
A chi-square test for independence
Three one-proportion z tests
A two-sample z test for the bus proportions

items.q: Which null hypothesis fits this test?

why.correct: $H_0$: the distributions are the same; $H_a$: at least one differs.
options: The test compares the travel mode distributions, not school sizes.
That is the alternative: at least one school's distribution differs.
Equal shares for each mode is not the claim. $H_0$ says the schools share one distribution, whatever it is.
Right: homogeneity means "same distribution" in every population.
The three schools have the same number of students
The distribution of travel mode is different at each school
Bus, car and walking are equally common at each of the schools
The travel mode distribution is the same at all three schools

items.q: If $H_0$ is true, what is the expected count of East students who walk or bike?

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. Use row total times column total over the grand total.
That splits the walkers equally among the schools, but the schools have different sample sizes.

items.q: Which statement checks the 10% condition for this test?

why.correct: 10%: each sample is less than 10% of its population when sampling without replacement.
options: That is not a condition. Expected counts are checked against 5.
That is not the condition. The 10% condition compares sample size with population size.
Right: with three samples drawn without replacement, check each against its own population.
The populations are the students at each school, not the district's adults.
Each expected count is at least 10% of its row total
At least 10% of each sample walks or bikes
Each sample is less than 10% of the students at its own school
The 400 students are less than 10% of the district's adults

items.q: Which of these changes to the table would make the chi-square statistic larger, with the totals kept the same?

why.correct: The statistic measures how far the observed counts are from what $H_0$ predicts.
options: Then each term is 0 and $\chi^2 = 0$, the smallest it can be.
Closer counts give smaller terms and a smaller $\chi^2$.
Reordering the rows changes no count, so $\chi^2$ is the same.
Right: $\chi^2$ adds up $\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$, so larger gaps between observed and expected give a larger value.
Expected counts that equal the observed counts
Observed counts that sit closer to their expected counts
Listing the schools in a different order
Observed counts farther from their expected counts

items.q: Why is an expected count equal to (row total)(column total) divided by the grand total?

options: Equal cells would ignore the totals. Expected counts follow the table's own row and column totals.
Multiplying, then dividing by the grand total, is not an average; it applies a proportion to a row.
Expected counts come from $H_0$ alone, not from making them match the data.
Right: the column proportion, column total over grand total, applies to every row, so expected = row total times that proportion.
It spreads the grand total equally over the cells of the table
It is the average of the row total and the column total
It makes the expected counts as close as possible to the observed counts in the table
With no association, each row shares the whole table's column proportions

items.q: A vet randomly assigns 150 dogs to three diets and records whether each dog's coat improves, stays the same or gets worse. Which test fits?

why.correct: Groups made by random assignment, one categorical response: homogeneity.
options: Right: randomly assigned groups are treated like separate samples, and one categorical outcome is compared across them.
That ignores the diets, the point of the study.
The vet created three groups by random assignment; comparing their outcome distributions is homogeneity.
A two-sample z test compares two proportions. Here there are three groups and three outcomes.
Homogeneity: compare the three diet groups' outcome distributions
A one-proportion z test for the share of dogs that improve
A chi-square test for independence, since the dogs form one group
A two-sample z test, since there are two variables

items.q: In a two-way table, one expected count is 3.2 and the rest are above 8. What does this mean for a chi-square test?

options: Right: every expected count must be at least 5.
Expected counts are not rounded, and rounding would not fix a small count.
The condition is on the expected count, which is 3.2 here.
Every expected count must reach 5, not most of them.
Large counts fails, so the p-value from the test may not be accurate
The 3.2 should be rounded to 3 before testing
The test is fine, as long as the observed count in that cell is above 5
The test is fine, because most of the expected counts are large

items.q: A student writes this alternative hypothesis for a test of independence: "$H_a$: there is an association, and people who exercise sleep more." What is wrong?

why.correct: $H_a$ for chi-square: there is an association (or the distributions differ), with no direction.
options: Right: the test cannot pick out a direction; follow-up work with the table can describe the association.
That is the null hypothesis.
Hypotheses are about the population, not the sample.
Recorded as categories (such as yes or no), exercise is categorical and fits a chi-square test.
A chi-square alternative only claims an association, with no direction
It should say there is no association between the variables
It should be written about the sample counts in the table
Exercise is not a categorical variable, so the test does not apply

items.q: A random sample of 200 workers is classified by whether they work from home (80 do, 120 do not) and whether they own a pet. Of those who work from home, 34 own a pet; of the others, 38 do. If working from home and pet ownership are independent, what is the expected count of workers who work from home and own a pet?

why.correct: 72 workers own a pet, so expected $= \frac{80 \times 72}{200} = 28.8$.

mistakes.why: That is the observed count. Expected $= \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}$.
That divides 200 equally over four cells. Use the totals: 80 work from home and 72 own a pet.

items.q: Which study calls for a chi-square test for independence rather than homogeneity?

why.correct: Independence: one sample, two variables. Homogeneity: several samples or groups, one variable.
options: Groups made by assignment, one outcome compared: homogeneity.
Right: one sample, two variables recorded on each voter.
Several samples, one variable: homogeneity.
Separate samples from each party, one variable compared: homogeneity.
Patients randomly assigned to three treatments, with the outcome recorded as better, same or worse
One random sample of 500 voters, each classified by party and by view on a ballot measure
Random samples of 100 students at four schools, asked their favorite subject
Separate random samples of 200 voters from each of three parties, asked their view on a measure
